sampleClaims.text: Dyslexia is predominantly characterized by a core deficit in phonological processing (the ability to recognize and manipulate speech sounds), which results in impairments in decoding (sounding out words), spelling, and word recognition.
sampleClaims.detailedDescription: This is the most widely accepted and empirically supported characterization of dyslexia's core deficit. Phonological processing involves the ability to recognize, remember, and manipulate the sounds of language (phonemes). This deficit manifests as difficulties in mapping letters to sounds (decoding), spelling words correctly, and recognizing words automatically.

sampleClaims.text: A cross-linguistic meta-analysis of 48 studies involving 1554 participants across Chinese logographic English deep alphabetic and German shallow alphabetic writing systems revealed universal neurobiological signatures of dyslexia characterized by convergent hypoactivation in the left fusiform gyrus and the inferior parietal lobule across languages. Language-specific reductions were identified the left inferior frontal gyrus in Chinese the left inferior temporal gyrus in English and the left inferior parietal lobule in German. Developmental meta-regressions demonstrated that in deep orthographic languages older children showed more convergent inferior temporal gyrus hypoactivation suggesting atypical ventral stream maturation. Conversely younger dyslexia children exhibited more convergent hypoactivation in the superior temporal gyrus in alphabetic languages indicating delayed dorsal stream development.

sampleClaims.text: Specific language impairment SLI is defined by the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders as a language disorder that interferes with the development of language skills in children who have no hearing loss or intellectual disabilities. The estimated prevalence of SLI in kindergarten students in the United States is 7.4 percent. Children with SLI comprise the majority of children with developmental language disorder and are at significantly increased risk of having reading disabilities. McArthur et al. found that 55 percent of dyslexic children recruited from schools or clinics also met the criteria for SLI and that 51 percent of children with SLI recruited from language development centers also met the criteria for dyslexia. SLI and dyslexia are different disorders that frequently co occur. Dyslexia is a disorder involving impaired word reading skills. Both disorders have a negative impact on reading comprehension and confer risks to broader academic achievement. Dyslexia has been strongly linked to difficulties in the phonological component of language. These phonological difficulties have been described as core deficits interfering with the mapping of phonemes to graphemes that is necessary for decoding new words and thereby playing a causal role in dyslexia.

sampleClaims.text: In a pre registered longitudinal fMRI study children oversampled for dyslexia risk were scanned in kindergarten prior to formal reading instruction and again in third grade. In region of interest analyses children who later developed dyslexia compared to controls showed reduced neural adaptation to written words in the left ventral occipito temporal cortex already in kindergarten despite matched pre reading skills. This result was confirmed in individually defined region of interest analyses and was restricted to the anterior part of the ventral occipito temporal cortex. The group difference remained stable across development. Across the full kindergarten sample adaptation to words in left ventral occipito temporal cortex was modestly associated with prereading skills including phonological awareness. No robust group differences were observed at the whole brain level or for non linguistic visual categories. These findings indicate small region specific differences in neural adaptation to print that are detectable prior to formal reading instruction.

sampleClaims.text: The International Dyslexia Association Board of Directors provided a definition in November 2002 stating Dyslexia is a specific learning disability that is neurological in origin. It is characterized by difficulties with accurate and or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities. These difficulties typically result from a deficit in the phonological component of language that is often unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities and the provision of effective classroom instruction. Secondary consequences may include problems in reading comprehension and reduced reading experience that can impede growth of vocabulary and background knowledge. This definition reflects the trend towards encompassing a number of traits within the dyslexia syndrome moving further away from a definition of dyslexia as primarily a deficit in reading abilities. Critchley in 1970 described dyslexia as a disorder manifested by difficulty in learning to read despite conventional instruction adequate intelligence and socio cultural opportunity depending on fundamental cognitive disabilities which are frequently of constitutional origin. The field of dyslexia has often been subject to controversy and contradictions. There are numerous official definitions that attempt to clarify an increasingly complex condition. A comprehensive review of research within the field pointed out the multiple and conflicting uses of the term and concluded that in dyslexia research and practice there is a degree of inconsistency verging on anarchy.

sampleClaims.text: The term dyslexia has seen a long history of interpretation and use. Before provision of a universally accepted definition of dyslexia in the Code of Practice by the Department of Education and Employment in 1994 some would use dyslexia to refer to either developmental dyslexia or learning difficulty. Before the start of 20th century dyslexia was regarded as medical irregularity and the term word blindness was commonly used to describe difficulties in reading and writing. Johannes Schmidt reported a case of reading difficulty caused by a stroke in 1676. Adolph Kussmaul called reading difficulties word blindness in 1887. Rudolf Berlin used the term dyslexia for the first time in 1887. The latest research evidence shows that reading disability is not an all or nothing deficiency but should be considered on a continuum starting from very low to very high. Nearly all individuals with a reading disability have similar symptoms most notably deficits in phonological processing. Deficiencies in semantics and syntax have not been found to be a primary cause of dyslexia. There is not a consensus about definitions and explanations of the concept of dyslexia with some people considering dyslexia a deficit and some seeing it as a different learning style. There is not a clear boundary between reading difficulties and other learning difficulties rooted in neurological and developmental impairments.

sampleClaims.text: The double-deficit hypothesis posits that both rapid naming and phonological impairments can cause reading difficulties, and that individuals with both deficits show greater reading impairments than those with a single deficit. fMRI evidence shows dissociation between brain regions sensitive to phonological awareness (left inferior frontal and inferior parietal regions) and rapid naming (right cerebellar lobule VI). The double-deficit group showed less activation in the frontoparietal reading network compared to children with only a phonological awareness deficit, who in turn showed less activation than typically-reading children. The double-deficit group also showed less cerebellar activation compared to children with only a rapid naming deficit. Functional connectivity analyses revealed that bilateral prefrontal regions were key for linking brain regions associated with phonological awareness and rapid naming, with the double-deficit group showing the most aberrant connectivity.

sampleClaims.text: Specific language impairment and dyslexia are separate yet frequently co occurring disorders that confer risks to reading comprehension and academic achievement. The estimated prevalence of specific language impairment in kindergarten students in the United States is 7.4 percent. Children with specific language impairment comprise the majority of children with developmental language disorder and are at significantly increased risk of having reading disabilities as well as experiencing difficulties in other academic areas including writing math and science. McArthur and colleagues found that 55 percent of dyslexic children recruited from schools or clinics also met the criteria for specific language impairment and that 51 percent of children with specific language impairment recruited from language development centers also met the criteria for dyslexia. These authors hypothesized that whether a child was diagnosed with dyslexia or specific language impairment depended more on who was giving the diagnosis than on specific characteristics of the child performance.

sampleClaims.text: The subtyping of dyslexic children proposed by Boder in 1971 and 1973 has been validated by quantitative neurophysiological techniques. Children were classified as being dysphonetic auditory phonetic disabilities dyseidetic visual spatial disabilities or mixed deficient in both processes. In one study of 21 dyslexic children between 7 and 10 years of age and six controlled children there were significant differences between the dyslexic subgroups and between the dyslexic and controlled children on three of the six cognitive tasks frustration level reading spelling recognition and drawing a clock. Significant differences occurred in left temporal parietal theta and this difference occurred in the area of the angular gyrus presumed to be important in phonetic decoding. This suggested that the reportedly normal phonetic skills of dyseidetic children may not be normal but rather a sign of overuse of a processing strategy associated with inefficiency of right hemisphere visual gestalt abilities. The Boder Test of Reading Spelling Patterns is a diagnostic screening test for subtypes of reading disability that identifies four subtypes on the basis of reading and spelling performance. The test is based on the premise that dyslexic readers have characteristic patterns of strengths and weaknesses in two distinct cognitive components of the reading process the visual gestalt function and the auditory analytic function.

sampleClaims.text: Within the amusia group 38 percent of participants exhibited dyslexia traits. Subgroup analyses distinguishing between individuals with pure amusia and those with amusia and comorbid dyslexia traits revealed that individuals with pure amusia still demonstrated difficulties in spoonerism and tone oddity but not in onset phoneme deletion and word reading. The amusia group as a whole showed segmental phonological awareness deficits under the low memory load condition and word reading deficits but these group level deficiencies were largely driven by the amusia subgroup with dyslexia traits. Hierarchical regression analyses showed that pitch height perception was a significant predictor of amusical participants performance in spoonerism and tone oddity. These findings highlight the importance of taking dyslexia status into account in amusia studies.

sampleClaims.text: Dyslexia prevalence is approximately 5% in adulthood, with estimates ranging from 1.6% to 6.4% among Spanish university students. Approximately 25% of children with dyslexia compensate in adulthood. Adults with compensated dyslexia performed similarly to controls in semantic verbal fluency, vocabulary, and word recognition accuracy, but showed significant differences in phonological awareness, low-frequency word reading, and technical text reading. Semantic verbal fluency and phonological awareness strongly determined membership in the non-compensated group. Speed performance on phonological tasks predicted speed reading in the compensated group for tasks involving the phonological reading route. Adults with compensated dyslexia have a smaller phonological deficit than non-compensated peers.

Socioeconomic status primarily predicted performance on tasks with higher lexical demands and nonverbal IQ. Once SES was considered, language background only influenced spelling tasks. Interaction effects indicated a stronger influence of SES in heritage bilinguals. These findings underscore the importance of SES in assessing heritage bilingual children and promoting the home language in clinical populations.

sampleClaims.text: Mathematics learning disorders and reading learning disorders each have an estimated prevalence of approximately 5 to 10 percent among school-age children. Their comorbidity is highly prevalent with around 40 percent of children with mathematics disorders also experiencing reading disorders. Comorbidity rates have been estimated at approximately 7.5 percent of the general population which exceeds the likelihood of an individual having both conditions purely by chance. Three hypotheses explain this comorbidity the additive model which proposes comorbidity results from the addition of neurocognitive deficits unique to each disorder the domain-general deficits model which proposes comorbidity stems from executive function deficits and the increased risk model which proposes comorbidity emerges from phonological deficits characteristic of reading disorders.

sampleClaims.text: Developmental dyslexia is a heritable learning disability affecting 7 to 10 percent of the general population. The prevalence is higher ranging from 40 to 60 percent among children with familial history of dyslexia than among those without familial history. In a cohort study of 98 infants with a mean age of 8.5 months multivariate pattern analyses identified distinct functional connectivity patterns between infants with versus without familial history of dyslexia in the left fusiform gyrus. Connections linking left fusiform gyrus to regions in the frontal and parietal language and attention networks were among the paths with the highest contributions to the classification performance. These findings suggest that familial history of dyslexia was associated with alterations in infant functional connectivity of key regions important for subsequent word recognition suggesting a potential early emergence of an atypical functional network underlying reading development.

sampleClaims.text: Dyslexia has a prevalence of 5 to 12 percent with prevalence varying by diagnostic criteria and cut-off points. Inherited factors are estimated to account for up to 80 percent of dyslexia depending on the phenotype dimension investigated with the highest estimates for word reading up to 58 percent and spelling 70 percent. Linkage findings are relatively consistent across studies particularly for chromosome regions 1p34 to p36 6p21 to p22 15q21 and 18q11. Four candidate genes have been identified through systematic linkage disequilibrium studies and cloning approaches. Results indicate that a disturbance in neuronal migration is a pathological correlate of dyslexia at the functional level.

sampleClaims.text: Dyslexia is the most prevalent learning disorder with a global prevalence among school aged children estimated at approximately 7 percent. In a task based fMRI study using hidden semi Markov models children with dyslexia spent significantly less time in a low integration brain state and more time in states characterised by stronger positive connectivity compared with typically developing children. The most highly integrated state was observed exclusively in the dyslexia group and accounted for a substantial proportion of scan time. Dyslexia was associated with altered sojourn duration distributions in two states including prolonged durations in an intermediate state and transition patterns biased toward increasingly integrated configurations whereas typically developing children more frequently transitioned back to the low integration state. These findings provide evidence that dyslexia is associated with altered dynamic functional connectivity within the sampled task constrained attention language system characterised by altered engagement across a graded integration segregation continuum and atypical temporal regulation of brain state transitions.

sampleClaims.text: A substantial number 41.3 percent of children with a family risk of dyslexia had received speech and language therapy. The nature of their difficulties did not differ in severity or form from those shown by other children receiving speech and language therapy. However both speech and language therapy and family risk of dyslexia were independent risk factors in predicting reading difficulties both concurrently and six months later. These results are best explained in terms of the multiple deficits model in which most developmental disorders occur as a result of multiple co-occurring deficits and comorbidity occurs because one or more of these deficits is shared between two disorders. sampleClaims.text: In a magnetoencephalography study investigating spatiotemporal neural responses during single word reading in typically developing and dyslexic children aged 7 to 12 direct comparisons between the groups revealed significant amplitude reductions in the dyslexia group across the bilateral occipito temporal and left superior temporal cortices. Despite these reduced signal amplitudes the inter hemispheric relationship of peak latencies in the dyslexia group remained consistent with the typically developing pattern. Within the typically developing group a clear relationship was identified between age and peak latency with older typical readers exhibiting decreased latencies in the left hemisphere pointing to the age related automatization of the reading network. In contrast this age related pattern was not observed in the dyslexia group which highlights a functional atypicality that remains evident across the investigated age range. These findings indicate that the core neural atypicality in dyslexia involves reduced activation strength and an absence of typical age related peak latency decreases rather than a fundamental overall shift in peak latency.
